The Coming Age of Robotic Warfare
item.description:
A battalion of armed robots moves against a unit of soldiers, aiming to seize territory. In the ensuing battle, the robots open fire, communicate with one another and change tactics as needed. Air cover is provided by uncrewed drones; logistical support and supplies are delivered by a separate team of robots. Territory is taken, prisoners captured. When the battle is over, the attacking side has lost several drones and robots, but no human beings have been killed or wounded.

Science fiction? Hardly. Some elements in this scenario – unmanned aerial cover and logistical support – are already commonplace in Ukraine. So are small-scale robot-led military actions. And experts say the other piece – robots leading major battlefield operations – is coming soon.

Ukraine's ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who led a warp-speed campaign to bring an “Army of Drones” to the battlefield, has launched what he calls a “Manhattan Project” to build an “Army of Robots.”

“The goal of the Robot Army is to save human lives,” Fedorov said in a recent presentation. “Robots should perform the most dangerous work so that our soldiers return home.”

“The main question for 2027 is not whether Ukraine will have an army of robots – it already does,” said Morgan, the commander of a Special Operations Group in the DIU (Defense Intelligence of Ukraine), who goes by his call name.

“The question is how quickly we can scale it up, and hand over to robots more of the tasks that people perform today at the risk of their own lives.”

It’s a brave new world of warfighting, and beyond its life-saving promise, it raises questions about non-human decision-making, and how widely and quickly AI-guided robots will displace the world’s soldiers.

“The premise has to be that there will be human control,” Lt. Gen. Jack Shanahan (Ret.), who served as the first director of the Defense Department’s Joint Artificial Intelligence Center, told The Cipher Brief.

“What we have to figure out is where, when and how that control gets applied. I do not want to see machines deciding…to do something that the humans never anticipated.”

Major Yabchanka’s Journey

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Oleksandr Yabchanka was a combat medic; today, he commands an unmanned systems platoon for the “Da Vinci Wolves” battalion, and specializes in what he calls “the robotization of combat processes.”

“The route a robot covers today is one that people would previously have had to cover,” Major Yabchanka told The Cipher Brief. “In our conditions, that would mean an extremely high risk of being hit. Robots take that risk upon themselves.”

Nearly every Ukrainian military unit now uses AI-guided robots, or UGVs (unmanned ground vehicles), for a range of mundane but dangerous tasks. Yabchanka described a supply chain that begins with human soldiers in rear positions who hand off ammunition, food and other supplies to UGVs for the proverbial last mile to the front. Robots repair cables and antennas, transfer munitions, and help armored vehicles that are stuck in the mud. And increasingly, they’ve been evacuating wounded soldiers.

“This is one of the most difficult operations, often carried out under intense fire,” Morgan, the Special Operations commander, told The Cipher Brief. “When robotic systems are used for evacuation, the risk is significantly reduced for service members who would otherwise have to go out to help their wounded comrades.” He believes that ground robots have already saved tens of thousands of lives.

“Imagine having to carry a wounded person ten kilometers,” Major Yabchanka said. “It takes a long time, it’s physically exhausting, and once detected, the evacuation team becomes a priority target. We risk losing both the wounded soldier and those who go to save him. That is why we hand this work over to UGVs.”

Ukraine's Defense Ministry reported in September that UGVs had carried out 112,000 logistics and casualty-evacuation missions this year.

“Many of the (scenarios) are no longer science fiction,” Major Yabchanka said. “The question is not so much whether an army of robots is possible, but how quickly we can bring these technologies to the required level of reliability, integrate them into combat processes and ensure their mass use.”

Robot soldiers that think

The holy grail in this robotic evolution is full-scale offensive operations. Call that Mykhailo Fedorov’s dream.

For the moment, battlefield decisions are still made by humans. Those casualty evacuations are overseen by a human operator; and no large “units” of robots have gone into battle alone.

But in small ways, Fedorov’s dream is already a reality.

The New York Times reported on a battle in the Kharkiv region featuring robotic vehicles which advanced on a Russian position – “little green wagons” that “looked like something you might buy at a garden store to move bags of soil.” Each vehicle carried 66 pounds of explosives, and as they neared the Russian troops, an aerial drone dropped a bomb and one of the robots blew itself up.

Two Russian soldiers soon emerged from a trench with a sign that read “We want to surrender.”

In other words, a robot-led attack had resulted in the capture of Russian prisoners. “It is better to throw in metal than people,” Lt. Mykola Zinkevych, who commanded the attack, told the Times. “Human life is precious, and robots don’t bleed.”

More recently, in Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Donbas, UGVs were dropped by aerial drones deep into Russian lines; the robots then attacked Russian positions. As one of Vivaldi’s commanders, who goes by “Darwin,” told The Cipher Brief, his men would establish a defense line and then wait “until artillery, flying drones and robots do their work, and then go in again.” Darwin said his corps was the first to demonstrate such coordination between autonomous and human elements.

David Kirichenko, an Associate Research Fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, said Vivaldi had demonstrated “the inexorable erosion of the usefulness of humans in direct contact with the enemy.”

In another recent milestone, Ukraine’s "Lava" Unmanned Systems Regiment carried out what it said was the world’s first combat logistics mission utilizing an AI-driven ground robot without human supervision. The Defense Ministry said its robot navigated 93 percent of a roughly 12-mile route; a human operator stepped in only for a one-mile stretch where the terrain differed from what mapping software had suggested.

Fedorov’s “Manhattan Project,” which he unveiled at a conference in Lviv in late September, would take all this to scale – battalions of “humanoid robots” that are given a mission and are able to adjust tactics in mid-battle. Swarms of aerial drones have already shown this capability; as Lt. Gen. Shanahan noted, “we’re talking about drone swarms on the ground as opposed to in the air.” Fedorov says his “Army of Robots” is a logical evolution in the autonomous weapons space, and a way to address Ukraine’s manpower shortage.

“We want to eventually substitute our infantry with these robots,” he said.

Fedorov’s plans are supported by a new consortium that includes outside investors including Palantir CEO Alex Karp. In a recent interview, Fedorov said the project had attracted more than 800 applications from companies, engineers, designers and programmers.

As with nearly all military innovation in Ukraine, the “Army of Robots” time horizon is ambitious. Fedorov’s presentation included an initial six-month phase culminating when a “humanoid robot” kills its first Russian soldier; within a year, he said, robots will be ready to conduct major coordinated assaults on their own.

“We don’t have enough time,” Fedorov told the Lviv conference. “We need to achieve these results as soon as possible.”

The Pentagon’s Push

Ukraine is now the widely-recognized global testing ground for new military technology, the home to what Cipher Brief expert and former CIA Director Gen. David Petraeus has referred to as “tomorrow's technology for today's wars.”

With this in mind, American manufacturers have sent prototypes of robotic soldiers to Ukraine. In June, San Francisco-based Foundation Future Industries said it had dispatched its Phantom Mk1 robots to Ukraine for battlefield testing. Foundation CEO Sankaet Pathak said he was “convinced the technology is reaching a level where it can replace jobs that are dangerous for humans to perform, and if you can do that, it’s the highest net good you can create out of all applications of robotics.”

Meanwhile, the U.S. and other countries are escalating efforts to boost robotic capabilities within their militaries. In late September, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the creation of an Autonomous Warfare Command, and called on all the services to accelerate their autonomous and robotic capabilities.

“We will fuse procurement with operations at scale,” Hegseth said, “and allow warfighters and engineers and entrepreneurs to learn, adapt, and rapidly iterate on their domain.”

“What we’re beginning to see with the U.S military is an increasing emphasis on autonomous systems on the ground side, the sea side and the air side,” Lt. Gen. Shanahan said. “I sense a palpable sense of urgency that I didn’t feel a couple of years ago.”

Experts say the urgency is driven by Ukraine’s successes as well as the possibility of conflict with China. China is developing sophisticated military robotic systems of its own, helped by an already-strong commercial robotics and electronics sector. Recently China showcased quadrupedal ground robots, or “robotic wolves,” which experts say are designed to cover rough and mountainous terrain. Beijing’s broader military strategy emphasizes “intelligentized warfare”; integrating AI, robotics, and data networks into combat operations.

Lt. Gen. Shanahan says such integration will be critical for the U.S. as it boosts its autonomous systems.

“Technically, it’s doable pretty quickly,” Shanahan said. “Organizationally, and the integration piece of it, these are hard things to work through.”

Risks and limitations

Questions abound about the future of robotic armies – not least, their reliability, mobility and ability to react under fire. “Humanoid robots” are expensive, mechanically complicated and – for the moment at least – far less sophisticated than conventional ground vehicles and drones.

“You still need to take ground and hold it to end a war, and both sides have to agree the war is over,” Shanahan said. “You can’t do that with drones on the ground...At some point you will need to end up putting humans on the ground to hold ground or push back.”

Among practical concerns, experts list communications, cost and coordination.

An operator cannot continuously control a robot if the adversary jams its radio links; Major Yabchanka has seen his UGVs frequently disabled by Russian electronic jamming. “For more complex autonomous functions,” he said, “more and more computing has to happen on board the robotic system itself, without depending on an external server or a continuous communication link. This requires additional computing power, sensors and power supply. All of this increases cost.”

In terms of coordination, large “units” of deployed robots must avoid collisions, particularly in a dynamic battlefield. As with other AI-driven systems, experts say repeated battlefield tests will help iron out such problems.

The most profound questions involve the human element. Will human beings remain in control of missions once they are launched? Will robot soldiers identify potential targets? And will robots or humans authorize engagement?

“We get so caught up in technology itself, we forget what the most important piece of it is,” Shanahan said. “How are you going to fight with it? What’s your operating concept? What’s your organizational design, for bringing in all these ground systems? Where do you want to put the humans, where do you want to put the machines?”

Shanahan raised one specific nightmare scenario: a robot unit that collectively “decides” that its mission is best served by striking a civilian target that no human has authorized.

“You could see this robot out there with agentic capability, deciding that the quickest way to end the war is not to hit this thing that the human wants it to hit, but to hit that hospital over there because the enemy will back down once 500 civilians are killed in a hospital off the battlefield,” Shanahan said. “That’s a catastrophe in the making.”

Even frontline commanders in Ukraine, who crave every technological edge they can get, share such concerns.

“Questions that once seemed like fiction are now becoming entirely practical,” Major Yabchanka said. “Today, in most of the systems we work with, the decision to use lethal force remains with the operator. But technology is already moving toward a point where that decision could be handed over to a machine…We could end up in a situation where the decision to kill a human being gradually ceases to be a human decision. This is a very dangerous stage of technological development, and humanity should not rush toward it.”

Morgan, the special operations commander, shares these concerns. But he also calls Ukraine’s AI-driven robots “one of our enormous advantages over Russia.”

Yabchanka agrees. “Robotization is not just a new technology,” he said. “It is our competitive advantage and one of the main paths to victory over an enemy with far greater manpower. This is not just a matter of technological progress. I am convinced that this is how we can win this war.”

item.title: Fire Base Australia: Can America’s Southern Base Sustain a Pacific War?
item.description:
American access to Australian bases is only as valuable as Australia’s ability to keep them operating under attack. For Washington, expanding military cooperation raises an operational question: can Australia sustain an American campaign while defending its own territory, infrastructure and population?

For Canberra, the corresponding question is whether investment in national resilience is keeping pace with Australia’s growing usefulness to American operations. Both governments need convincing answers before a regional crisis turns access arrangements into wartime demands.

The benefits are considerable. Australian facilities offer strategic depth, logistical support and opportunities to disperse forces. Australia gains access to American capabilities, intelligence and interoperability. Their wartime value, however, depends on protection, sustainment and the host country’s continued ability to function.

The 2026 Iran war offers a warning. Despite America’s regional military presence, Gulf partners suffered casualties, damage and disruption from Iranian attacks. The lesson is not that every incoming weapon must be intercepted. It is that defending individual facilities and sustaining the country around them are different tasks.

Australia differs substantially from the Gulf states. Nevertheless, an adversary could seek to weaken an American campaign by imposing costs on its Australian support network. A base might remain operational while disruption to surrounding energy, transport and civilian services progressively reduces its usefulness.

Australia could face three simultaneous responsibilities: supporting American operations, contributing combat forces and defending its homeland. Aircraft assigned to coalition missions might also be needed to protect Australian approaches. Maritime forces could face competing demands to support forward operations and secure essential supply routes. Fuel, munitions and maintenance capacity would serve all three responsibilities.

These tensions matter directly to Washington. Disruption could reduce sortie generation, delay replenishment and constrain repairs. Requests for additional protection could divert American forces from other missions. Civilian hardship could generate political pressure over the scale or conditions of continued Australian support.

This is a planning problem, not a prediction that Australia would abandon its ally. Alliance planning should make such pressure difficult to exploit.

The ANZUS Treaty provides a commitment to meet common danger through each country’s constitutional processes. It does not allocate the forces, stockpiles or repair capacity needed to sustain Australia under attack. Those arrangements require practical agreement.

Canberra carries substantial responsibility. It cannot expand its supporting role while assuming Washington will supply whatever protection becomes necessary. Australia’s 2026 National Defence Strategy emphasizes greater self-reliance, industrial resilience and civil preparedness. The test is whether implementation can sustain national defense and alliance operations simultaneously.

Washington must likewise distinguish access from assured capacity. American forces operating from Australia may have missions elsewhere; their presence should not automatically be counted as an equivalent addition to Australian territorial defense. Reassigning them would carry consequences for the wider campaign.

The Wartime Planning Dilemma

Consider a Taiwan conflict later this decade in which the United States intervenes and Australia provides access, logistical support and a limited combat contribution while defending itself. This is a planning scenario, not a forecast. Proposed facilities must be assessed separately from capabilities already available.

Northern airfields, including Darwin and Tindal, could support aircraft rotations, staging, refueling and maintenance. Upgrades at Tindal to accommodate American bombers increase its potential utility. But aircraft parking capacity does not determine sustained combat output. Fuel distribution, munitions handling, maintenance personnel and runway repair would govern how frequently aircraft could operate.

Southern Australia offers additional depth. Reported plans for a Marine Corps prepositioning facility in Victoria, expected to reach full capacity in 2028, illustrate the value of storing equipment away from northern operating locations. Distance can reduce exposure to some threats while increasing transport requirements and replenishment times.

Such facilities also require planning with surrounding communities. Targeting exposure, hazardous fuel and ammunition storage, and pressure on civilian roads, utilities and emergency services must all be assessed. Local preparedness is part of operational resilience.

In Western Australia, HMAS Stirling could support submarine operations and sustainment. Its contribution would depend on qualified personnel, specialist facilities and available components, rather than port access alone. Joint facilities, including Pine Gap’s intelligence and missile-warning functions and Harold E. Holt’s submarine communications, add capabilities whose disruption could affect operations far beyond Australia.

The threat should be assessed across three overlapping tiers. These describe the expanding scope of disruption, not a predictable escalation sequence.

Tier one: military capability. Attacks on airfields, naval facilities, logistics installations or communications could reduce operational output without destroying entire bases. Planners should test combinations of physical attack, cyber disruption and sabotage. Concentrating essential functions at a few locations creates dependencies that dispersal, hardening, redundancy and rapid repair must address.

The relevant measure is how much military activity survives and how quickly lost capacity returns. An intact runway offers limited value if fuel cannot reach aircraft or maintenance systems are unavailable.

Tier two: the civilian systems sustaining military operations. Electricity, telecommunications, commercial ports, roads and fuel distribution connect military facilities to the national economy. Their disruption could constrain operations even where bases escape direct attack. Several modest interruptions could combine into a serious loss of capacity.

Fuel illustrates the problem. Canberra’s 2026 fuel-security package includes a A$3.2 billion government reserve and measures intended to lift diesel and aviation-fuel reserves to 50 days. This is an important investment, but a national stockholding target does not establish endurance under wartime consumption or guarantee delivery to the facilities needing it.

Tier three: national endurance and political decision-making. Prolonged disruption could place military requirements in competition with hospitals, food distribution, civilian transport and essential industry. Shipping interruptions could compound domestic damage. The resulting hardship could become a means of coercion, whether or not civilian suffering was the initial purpose of an attack.

Deliberate attacks on population centers would represent an additional, grave contingency. They are not necessary for this tier to emerge: disruption to shared infrastructure could already produce substantial civilian harm. Planning must therefore include essential-service continuity, emergency communications and support for affected communities, alongside military recovery.

Across all three tiers, the central question is the same: how much pressure can Australia absorb while sustaining its agreed contribution?

Turning Access into Endurance

The answer requires decisions before hostilities. Both governments should establish which functions each facility can sustain, for how long, and under what assumptions about replenishment and damage. Planned capacity should enter campaign calculations only when it is available, staffed and exercised.

The United States Studies Centre has recommended prioritizing the “five R’s” of logistics—refuel, rearm, resupply, repair and revive—through the Combined Logistics Sustainment and Maintenance Enterprise announced at the 2021 Australia–U.S. Ministerial Consultations. This provides an existing foundation for stronger sustainment arrangements.

The additional requirement is to test those arrangements against simultaneous homeland-defense and civilian-continuity demands. Logistics cooperation alone cannot settle who protects facilities or who receives scarce resources.

First, the allies should agree protection responsibilities and procedures for allocating scarce aircraft, fuel, munitions, transport and repair capacity. Australian homeland defense, Australian combat deployments and American operations cannot each assume first call on the same resources. Governments must retain decision-making authority, but the trade-offs should be understood beforehand.

Second, investment should address the dependencies that most constrain sustained output: alternative distribution routes, dispersed reserves, repair teams, replacement components and resilient communications. Additional operating capacity should be matched by the capacity to protect, supply and restore it.

Third, joint exercises should test concurrent disruption across military installations and civilian networks. State governments, infrastructure operators and emergency services should participate where relevant. Exercises should measure sustained output and recovery times under delayed replenishment, rather than merely demonstrate that forces can deploy.

Neither government needs to disclose classified plans to make these priorities visible in budgets and preparedness programs.

A resilient Australia gives Washington more dependable operational options and reduces emergency reinforcement demands. An exposed Australia could require additional protection precisely when American forces are most heavily committed elsewhere.

The alliance’s southern base will be judged by what it can sustain under pressure. Australian resilience must therefore be treated as an essential input to American campaign planning, with responsibilities agreed, resources funded and recovery exercised before war begins.

item.title: The Hidden Cost of America’s War With Iran
item.description:
“The [U.S. Naval Support Activity Bahrain] base and Fifth Fleet headquarters have been rendered largely inoperable for their original functions, with repairs estimated at $400 million… Chief of Naval Operations Admiral Daryl Caudle and other senior defense officials stated that the Navy will not return to full normal operations at the Bahrain facility anytime soon…Because the Juffair surrounding area [to the U.S. Bahrain Navy facilities] is considered unsafe, [U.S. Navy] major logistical and port-call operations have been rerouted over 2,000 miles away to the Naval Support Facility Diego Garcia and other alternative hubs, causing significant resupply delays.”

That is an excerpt from a 19-page Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report titled, Estimating the Cost of Combat Operations Against Iran, sent to Congress September 15.

I read the now-seven-week-old CBO report last week, and was surprised at how much new-to-me information it contained about the early days of the Iran war, and particularly Tehran’s early destruction of U.S. military infrastructure which, up-to-recently, had not had much publicity in this country.

For example, although the U.S. attacks along with Israel on Iran began before dawn February 28, 2026, there apparently was a lack of expectation for the size of Iran counterattacks with missiles and drones that actually took place later that same day, February 28, in Bahrain and at other U.S. bases in Qatar, Kuwait, Jordan, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates.

And while the White House and Pentagon repeatedly have described the destruction U.S. and Israeli forces have done to Iran’s military, there has been as almost no mention of what was happening to the U.S. facilities.

In mid-September, the Defense Department (DoD) Inspector General (IG), as Lead IG, released a report on Operation Epic Fury (OEF) -- the war against Iran. The IG report found that “Iranian strikes damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict,” as of June 30, 2026, and the DoD had “$3.7 billion in equipment losses, but [that] does not include costs for infrastructure repairs.”

The IG report later noted it “did not include the cost of military construction for damaged infrastructure in its estimate because [DoD] has not determined what its future posture will be in the region, how it will construct its bases, and what percentage of the construction costs Allies and partners will contribute.”

On the other hand, the IG report did say “damage to U.S. embassies, consulates, and other diplomatic facilities had already cost the U.S. approximately $184 million.”

I should point out that the CBO September report, sent to Congress one day after the IG report was released, noted that DoD had failed to provide to it, the CBO, with an estimate on the cost of the damage to U.S. bases and facilities.

In fact, there still has yet to be any publicly-released official DoD estimate of the cost of damage to U.S. military bases and facilities based on Iran’s attacks.

However, Iran attacks in those first days of the war continued in a scale and duration that appeared to have taken the U.S. government by surprise. For example, it was not until March 2, the third day after attacks began, before the Navy and the State Department ordered the evacuation of dependents from Bahrain.

The September CBO report said, “Military families and non-essential personnel were evacuated [from Bahrain] in March 2026, and remain displaced across temporary housing, awaiting the eventual retrieval of personal belongings left behind…[and] Evacuated families have faced added strain as military leadership noted that temporary evacuation financial support is scheduled to conclude on November 30, 2026, even though shipping personal effects is expected to take several more months.”

Also indicating a surprise from Iran’s military response, the DoD’s IG report noted, “Prior to OEF, Bahrain had been U.S. Navy Central’s main logistics hub to sustain operations in the Persian Gulf region, USCENTCOM [U.S. Central Command] said. During major combat operations, Iran targeted Bahrain with [drones] and ballistic missile strikes. USCENTCOM stated that it initially shifted naval sustainment resources from Bahrain to alternate hubs.”

The IG Report added, “The establishment of adequate naval bases and support ports posed significant challenges before and during OEF, arising from complexities and due to uncertainties with host nation access permissions to utilize ports for fleet resupply, USCENTCOM said.”

For example, the need to shift logistics support and infrastructure to Diego Garcia added 14-to-18 days for transporting material by sea, according to the IG report.

As for the U.S. Combined Air and Space Operations Center (CAOC) at Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, the Air Force had since 2019 periodically conducted tests and temporary shifts of its operations to Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina to demonstrate distributed command-and-control capabilities and reduced reliance on a single point of failure.

As reported in June by Air and Space Forces Magazine, personnel were transferred away from Al Udeid before February 28. Therefore, when Iran weapons struck the COAC facility at Al Udeid Air Base in the early days of the war, operations were already being run out of Shaw Air Force Base.

Then, there is the already publicized, but apparently un-planned, heavy use of both offensive and defensive U.S. weaponry caused by the Iran war.

For example, the September CBO report estimated, “The cost to replace the munitions expended through August 1, 2026, is $21.7 billion: $7.3 billion for the land-attack cruise missiles, $13.1 billion for the missile defense interceptors, and $1.2 billion for other munitions. Replacing those munitions has been the largest single component of the costs incurred by DoD during the conflict.”

CBO estimated that it “would probably take at least five years” to replace certain interceptors even at an increased rate of production.

An October 5, Congressional Research Service (CRS) report, U.S. Military Operations Against Iran’s Missile and Nuclear Programs, raises another point worth considering -- whether the Trump planners understood the difficulty they faced in trying to disarm Iran.

The CRS report noted that President Trump on February 28, listed among the OEF’s objectives was destroying Iran’s missiles, and “[razing] their missile industry to the ground.”

However, as CRS reported following the initial U.S./Israeli attacks, “DIA [the Defense Intelligence Agency] assessed in April 2026 that Iran ‘retains thousands of missiles and one-way attack UAVs [drones] that can threaten U.S. and partner forces throughout the region, despite degradations to its capabilities from both attrition and expenditure.’”

CRS also reported articles that said “that Iran may have begun rebuilding military infrastructure, restoring access to missile bases, and resuming missile production using stockpiled components. An Iranian official reportedly asserted in August that Iran has sufficient ‘stockpiles in our underground missile and drone cities’ to enable continued production.”

The CRS report suggested Congress consider directing the Pentagon to produce an “annual report on military power of Iran,” along with a public version of that report.

While dealing with public reporting, I must note the odd way DoD has been handling public disclosure of U.S. dead and wounded since February 28, a system clearly designed to lower the numbers.

Instead of having one category, there are two – one for the period February 28-to-July 6, covering OEF with 15 deaths and 417 wounded; the second from July 7-to-present in a second category, “overseas operations,” which lists eight deaths and 448 wounded.

The Trump administration rationale was that a temporary ceasefire or memorandum of understanding was reached to end OEF and that fighting resumed on July 7, after the earlier ceasefire collapsed.

However, as Stars and Stripes reported last Thursday, “The Pentagon has revised the number of U.S. troops who have died during operations related to the war against Iran to 23… Additionally, 865 American service members have been wounded.”

Now we are in a period where President Trump has threatened, after today’s elections, to renew attacks on Iran. He has amassed a battle force that could carry it out. He has also warned allies in the region it may be coming.

The State Department has ordered nonessential government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia and made staffing adjustments or family departures across several diplomatic missions in the Middle East.

But as I have indicated above, Iran, which has the largest armed forces in the region, has a capability to strike back, whether the Pentagon acknowledges that or not.

Iran has developed a defense industry and its own military capabilities, including extensive underground facilities, and dispersal of munitions inventories.

The volume of U.S. offensive and defensive ammunition used so far against Iran show that any U.S. renewing of attacks to force Tehran to accept Washington’s terms, would not be a day or two operation.

And perhaps just as important to think about -- given what Ukraine has shown -- explosive drones can be launched toward targets thousands of miles away, showing no country is completely safe, no matter how far its borders are from the enemy.

item.title: China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one
item.description:
China and its trading partners are moving towards an economic peace. But it is a fragile one Expert comment thilton.drupal 3 November 2026

Beijing appears to have embraced economic stability in its relations with the US and the EU. But serious challenges over its currency and export model remain.

In a world full of geopolitical tension and war, it is worth pausing to consider the few signs of hope that have emerged these last few months in China’s relations with the US and the EU. 

Last month’s deal between Beijing and the EU to limit Europe’s imports of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs) is the most recent notable example. It represents an easing of trade tension and could help to defuse the threat of some very hostile trade tools that the French and German governments are now willing to deploy. 

This EU-China agreement also comes in the context of President Xi and President Trump agreeing to a period of ‘constructive strategic stability’ during Trump’s visit to China in May. While this apparent embrace of stability is welcome, China’s economic relations with its global trading partners remain contentious.

Self-serving stabilization

China has some very good reasons of its own to seek a period of stabilization. Just about the one thing that the US, the EU and many parts of the Global South can all agree on, these days, is their shared view that China should import more and export less. Beijing is immensely lucky that its trading partners can’t turn that common view into a common policy, and so they remain entirely uncoordinated in their response to China’s rapidly increasing share of the global market for manufactured goods. Beijing should worry that this luck may run out, and so it makes sense for the authorities there to offer some help. 

Related work

‘China shock 2.0’ and Europe’s industrial future

China’s reaction to the Hormuz crisis is another example of the ‘strategic reasonableness’ that Beijing seems to have adopted. China reduced its oil imports very sharply after Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March and threatened the world with the loss of some 12 million barrels per day of oil that couldn’t find alternative routes out of the region. In June this year, China’s oil imports were down by about 5 million barrels a day. This reduced stress in the world’s oil market, which both supported economic activity and helped minimize global inflationary pressures.

It should go without saying that self-interest was at work here. China’s intensely export-oriented growth model requires Beijing to make sure that the chokepoint leverage that it is amassing through its manufacturing dominance doesn’t lead to a catastrophic loss of trust on the part of its trading partners. And at a more basic level, China’s economic model requires its customers to stay afloat. Whatever Beijing can do to stabilize global demand conditions, it should do. And that’s not to mention the chance that rising populism in the West might take on a more explicitly anti-China hue in the future.

Fragility

It has to be said, though, that this stabilization is very fragile. For example, China’s agreement to limit its exports of PHEVs to Europe, albeit through a WTO-compliant ‘safeguard measure,’ runs several risks. One is that China’s other trading partners might wonder why Beijing offered export restraint to the EU but not them, potentially leading them to push for their own arrangements.

And within the EU, there seems to be a strong sense that now Beijing has agreed to restrain vehicles exports, the same kind of pressure could be applied to sectors like pharmaceuticals, chemicals and machinery. China’s tolerance for this might be very limited.

Moreover, Europe and China’s other trading partners have ‘whack-a-mole’ problem when it comes to Chinese manufactured exports. The main reason that a rise in PHEV exports became so visible is thanks to the tariffs that the EU imposed on battery electric vehicles two years ago: China simply boosted its exports of PHEVs which weren’t subject to the tariffs. Now that these will be constrained, it probably won’t be long before another kind of manufactured exports surge next.

Currency concerns

Another reason to curb one’s enthusiasm is the way in which the debate about global trade imbalances is likely to evolve.  

Beijing’s commitment to its manufacturing-led growth model seems, for the time being, unshakeable. What’s more likely is that China will agree to let its currency strengthen. 

Last month, France and Germany made it clear in their unofficial ‘non-paper’ on trade that an appreciation of the renminbi would be a tolerable substitute in the short term for a more meaningful economic rebalancing of the economy that would boost China’s spending on imports. More pressure on China might grow when the US Treasury publishes its next report on potential ‘currency manipulators’ early next year. 

It is difficult to argue against the idea that the renminbi remains highly undervalued. CF40, a distinguished Chinese economics think-tank, recently suggested that the underlying equilibrium exchange rate of the renminbi against the US dollar – adjusting for the fact that the cost of living in China is much lower – is around 2.5 CNY per USD. The current market exchange rate is just below 6.7.

In this respect, though, China’s trading partners should be careful what they wish for. A more expensive renminbi will inevitably boost inflationary pressures among China’s trading partners. The European Central Bank has shown how cheap imports from China have kept goods inflation more moderate than it would otherwise be. At a time when anxiety about inflation is especially acute, given the surge in prices seen since the Iran war started in February, a renminbi-induced inflation shock in Europe and the US may not be very welcome.

‘Safe’ FDI

Economic relations between China and its trading partners in the EU and the US suffer from a familiar security dilemma: my pursuit of security leaves you feeling less secure, and vice versa. 

The most hopeful way out of this might be for everyone to agree that China should increase its flow of ‘safe’ foreign direct investment (FDI) to the rest of the world. 

Want to hear more on the future of global trade?

Join us at our Global Trade Conference for expert analysis on the shifting rules of the global economy.

This issue is now at the centre of talks in Europe about the European Commission’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act. Bigger FDI flows would help to lower China’s trade surplus by generating production in host countries, along with all the benefits of local job creation, technology transfer and tax revenues. 

China has a long-term incentive to park industrial assets offshore, not least because they will generate a flow of cross-border investment income in the future.  

Finding a way to increase China’s FDI flow to Europe without causing conniptions about national security risks is a worthy task. Set against the $350 billion trade deficit the EU will run with China this year, China’s FDI annual inflows of around $10 billion are tiny. 

But boosting Chinese FDI will require tolerance of some minimal level of insecurity on Europe’s part. Otherwise, the pursuit of absolute security will come at an economic price that is just too high, and will, in the end, be self-defeating. FDI may well be the best way to build on the economic peace that is trying to break out.

item.title: Even if US democracy can be salvaged from Trump, Europe is moving on | Rafael Behr
item.description:
It will take decades to rebuild trust in a country that removed a tyrant once – and then reinstated him four years later

When Joe Biden entered the White House in 2021 it was possible to believe that Donald Trump’s reign had been an aberration. “America is back. The transatlantic alliance is back,” the new president declared to relieved European leaders shortly after winning the 2020 race. It was true, but not for long.

Trump’s defeat proved that US democracy was mechanically operational, not culturally robust. His supporters tried violent subversion to prevent the inauguration of a successor. A second term should have been unthinkable. Republicans who failed to denounce the 6 January insurrection should have been unelectable. Instead, within four years, US voters reinstated the champion of a failed coup against their cherished constitution as commander-in-chief.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Faruk Ahmed appointed new SRB DG
item.description:
Faruk Ahmed, additional inspector general (additional IGP) of Bangladesh Highway Police, has been appointed as the new director general (DG) of the Special Response Battalion (SRB).
The Ministry of Home Affairs issued a notification in this regard on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Md Ahsan Habib Palash, director general of the Special Response Battalion, has been transferred to the Police Headquarters in Dhaka.
A 17th BCS (Police) officer, Faruk joined the Bangladesh Police as an Assistant Superintendent of Police (ASP) in 1998.
The Special Response Battalion formally begun its operations on September 16 as a specialised unit of Bangladesh Police following the publication of the Special Response Battalion (SRB) Act, 2026 in the gazette.
Besides, Additional Inspector General of Police Md Sayedur Rahman of Police Headquarters has been transferred to the Highway Police.
Deputy Inspector General (DIG) Md Ashique Sayed has been appointed as the commissioner of Gazipur Metropolitan Police (GMP).
Meanwhile, incumbent GMP Commissioner Md Israil Hawlader has been promoted to Additional IGP and posted to the Industrial Police. Additional IGP Gazi Jasim Uddin of the Industrial Police has been transferred to the Police Telecom Organisation, Dhaka.
DIG Mir Ashraf Ali, who was serving in the Railway Police, has been posted to the Rajshahi Range, replacing Ashique Sayed, who was serving as its DIG.
All the transfers and postings would take effect immediately, said the notification.

DU leads Bangladesh in QS Asia rankings
item.description:
The University of Dhaka (DU) has retained its position as Bangladesh’s top-ranked university in the QS World University Rankings: Asia 2027, although it slipped four places to 136th in the regional rankings compared with last year.
The rankings were released on Tuesday by international higher education ranking agency Quacquarelli Symonds (QS), featuring more than 1,720 universities across 26 higher education systems.
North South University (NSU) ranked second among Bangladeshi universities, retaining its 149th position in Asia. Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) placed third nationally, dropping 14 places to 179th.
A total of 52 Bangladeshi universities featured in this year’s rankings, taking the country’s representation above 50 for the first time. In 2017, only two Bangladeshi universities were included.
According to QS, 12 Bangladeshi universities improved their positions, seven retained their previous rankings and 27 slipped. Six institutions made their debut. However, the number of Bangladeshi universities among Asia’s top 500 fell from 16 last year to 14.
Daffodil International University advanced five places to 216th, while BRAC University dropped 11 places to 271st. Jahangirnagar University fell 25 places to 329th, and Rajshahi University slipped 37 places to 349th.
Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) made a significant improvement, climbing 44 places to 370th. Bangladesh Agricultural University retained its 378th position.
Gazipur Agricultural University, formerly Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Agricultural University, entered Asia’s top 500 for the first time, ranking 407th.
The QS report said Bangladeshi universities performed relatively well in the citations per paper indicator. Three local universities ranked among Asia’s top 10 in this category, while 10 made it into the top 100. Bangladesh ranked fifth in Asia based on the average score in this indicator.
However, the report highlighted weaknesses in faculty-student ratios, the proportion of academic staff holding PhDs, international faculty and student exchange programmes. No Bangladeshi university made Asia’s top 200 in any of these indicators.
Among Asian universities, the University of Hong Kong topped the rankings, followed by Peking University of China. Tsinghua University, also in China, climbed six places to third.

item.title: PM orders advancing plans for 2nd Padma, Jamuna bridges and Padma Barrage
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Tuesday directed officials to advance plans for a second Padma Bridge, a second Jamuna Bridge and the Padma Barrage, prioritising improved connectivity in the southwestern and northern regions.
He gave the directives at a meeting with officials of the relevant ministries and divisions at the Prime Minister’s Office in the Bangladesh Secretariat in the afternoon, said PM’s Assistant Press Secretary Abdullah Al Mahmud Shahriar.
The meeting was informed that feasibility studies for the second Padma and Jamuna bridges are underway.
Final decisions on their locations, designs and estimated costs will be made after the studies are completed in September next year.
The proposed second Padma Bridge was discussed with a focus on a Y-shaped connection system, while improved connectivity for Rangpur and other northern districts was highlighted in planning the second Jamuna Bridge.
The second Padma Bridge, if built, will improve communication between the capital and the southwestern region.
It will also provide alternative connectivity to Mongla seaport and the Benapole and Darshana land ports.
The meeting also discussed the Padma Barrage project, including its potential to address dry-season water shortages, boost agricultural production, maintain river flows and environmental balance, and create road connectivity across the barrage.
Issues relating to project financing, land acquisition, rehabilitation and coordination among the relevant ministries and agencies also came up for discussion.
Road Transport and Bridges, Railways and Shipping Minister Shaikh Rabiul Alam, State Minister for Local Government, Rural Development and Co-operatives Mir Shahe Alam, State Minister for Railways and Road Transport and Highways Habibur Rashid, State Minister for Water Resources Farhad Hossain Azad and State Minister for Shipping and Bridges Division Md Razib Ahsan attended the meeting.
Finance Secretary Dr Md Khairuzzaman Majumder, Bridges Division Secretary Mohammad Abdur Rauf, Water Resources Secretary Dr AKM Shahabuddin, Road Transport and Highways Division Secretary Dr Mohammad Ziaul Haque and other senior officials were also present.

item.title: U.S. job postings rose sharply in September
item.description:
U.S. employers ramped up their job postings in September as stronger economic growth may be encouraging more hiring. Yet voters are headed to the polls Tuesday, largely gloomy over an economy beset by higher prices.

U.S. job openings jumped to 7.5 million from a revised 7.19 million in August, the Labor Department reported Tuesday. It is the largest number of openings since May and up from a recent low of 6.9 million in March.

The department’s Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) also showed that gross hiring—job gains before subtracting people who quit or lost jobs—rose and layoffs fell in September.

The increases are a hopeful sign that hiring could improve, but the trend would have to continue for several months to suggest real progress. Hiring has been sluggish for nearly three years, though layoffs have also been historically low, a sign of meager “churn” in the labor market. Low churn means those who are employed are enjoying relatively high levels of job security, but it is much harder than normal for those looking for work to find a job.

Still, the number of job openings now exceeds the number of unemployed, a sharp switch from a year ago when there were more people out of work than available jobs.

“It’s an encouraging sign that despite all the headwinds right now with high diesel and gas prices and ongoing inflation problems, companies are slowly increasing their hiring,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said.

Job openings rose the most in professional and business services, which includes high-paying jobs in engineering and accounting, as well as jobs in the temp industry. Manufacturers, shipping firms, and state and local governments also advertised for more workers.

Nicole Bachaud, a labor economist at ZipRecruiter, cautioned that with inflation still high and interest rates having increased since the summer, companies may not be able to ramp up hiring by much in the coming months.

“All of that added up together just makes it much more expensive to operate as a business and much more expensive to expand,” she said. “And so that will likely continue to be a downward pressure on hiring, until we see inflation really able to cool down.”

The government will issue the October jobs report on Friday, which is forecast to show that employers added 65,000 positions last month, according to data provider FactSet. That would be an improvement from 29,000 in September. The unemployment rate is expected to stay at a low 4.2%.

Typically, job gains of just 65,000 would be seen as a sign of a struggling economy, but with the giant baby boom generation retiring and immigration sharply reduced, the economy doesn’t need to generate as many jobs as it has in the past for unemployment to remain low.

In September, layoffs fell sharply to just 1.64 million, the fewest since March 2025. The number of people quitting their jobs rose to 3.37 million, the highest in about 18 months, and up from 3.04 million.

The rise in quits is generally a good sign because workers usually leave a job when they either have another lined up or when they are confident they can find new work.

—Christopher Rugaber, AP economics writer

item.title: Democratic Congress could test decades of US support for Israel
item.description:
By Patricia Zengerle

WASHINGTON, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Democrats’ takeover of Congress and growing Republican unease over Israel could trigger the biggest reassessment of US support for its closest Middle East ally in decades, after an election shaped in part by anger over the Iran war.

Democrats won both the Senate and House in Tuesday’s midterms. Many winning candidates were progressives who campaigned against military aid to Israel and the US-Israeli war on Iran.

item.title: Morocco says it will uphold Western Sahara ceasefire after UN mission ends
item.description:
By Ahmed Eljechtimi

RABAT, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Morocco will stay committed to the ceasefire in Western Sahara despite the end of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in the territory, the Royal Palace said on Wednesday.

The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission came to an end after the Security Council did not renew its mandate last week, the UN said on Sunday, removing the international presence that has monitored the ceasefire in the decades-old dispute.

item.title: Red Cross delivers essential medical supplies to Yemen's besieged Taiz city
item.description:
By Olivia Le Poidevin

GENEVA, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The Red Cross said on Wednesday it had delivered four truckloads of essential medical supplies to the besieged Yemeni city of Taiz after renewed fighting cut off access for weeks.

Taiz has been largely isolated for a month, with fighting preventing humanitarian supplies from entering the city and restricting the movement of civilians, after an escalation in clashes between the Saudi-backed government and the Iran-aligned Houthi movement.

item.title: Turkey says EU comments on its rights record, judiciary are 'prejudiced, unfair'
item.description:
